 1                                      INTRODUCTION

 2   Q.   Please state your name and business address.

 3   A.   My name Peterson Brossy. My business address is the New Mexico Public Regulation

 4        Commission (“Commission” or “NMPRC”), 1596 Pacheco St, Santa Fe, NM 87505.

 5

 6   Q.   What is your position with the Commission?

 7   A.   I am a Public Utilities Economist in the Accounting Bureau of the NMPRC Utility Division

 8        Staff (“Staff”).

 9

10   Q.   Did you previously file Direct testimony in this case?

11   A.   Yes, my prepared Direct testimony was filed in this case on May 1, 2026.

12

13   Q.   What is the purpose of this testimony?

14   A.   My testimony provides discussion regarding why Staff was not a signatory to the

15        Stipulation filed in this case on June 22, 2026. My testimony also addresses certain

16        accounting-related provisions of the Stipulation.

17

                                   CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                       TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO STIPULATION OF
                                   PETERSON BROSSY

 1                            SUMMARY OF THIS TESTIMONY

 2   Q.   Please summarize your overall position regarding the Stipulation

 3   A.   While the Stipulation reflects positive movement from SPS's original proposal in certain

 4        respects, it does not adequately address the concerns Staff raised in its Direct testimony.

 5        The revenue deficiency of $90,000,000 is still significantly larger than Staff’s

 6        recommended deficiency of $47,691,101. Staff Witness Jonah Mauldin addresses the

 7        revenue requirement total amount in his Testimony in Opposition to the Stipulation. Staff’s

 8        positions on the Stipulation’s specific terms addressed in this testimony are summarized

 9        below.

10        The return on the Deferred Tax Asset (“DTA”) from solar Production Tax Credits (“PTCs”)

11        is reduced from SPS’s original request to the long-term cost of debt but is still above Staff’s

12        Direct testimony recommendation of weighted average cost of debt. The Stipulation also

13        includes language to pass the return to the Company through the FPPCAC. Staff

14        recommends the return on the DTA instead be included in base rates. Regarding Investment

15        Tax Credit items from the Cunningham BESS and Plant X BESS (“ITC”), Staff

16        recommends no return on the transaction costs accrued in a regulatory asset, instead of the

17        WACC return as stated in the Stipulation.

18        The proposed Stipulation rate case expense is unreasonably high and should be adjusted to

19        $3.3 million from $4.3 million. Also, the amortization period should be three years instead

20        of two, as Staff recommended in my Direct testimony.




                                                    2
                                           CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                               TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO STIPULATION OF
                                           PETERSON BROSSY

 1              Regarding regulatory assets, the remaining investment in legacy meters should be

 2              amortized over five years instead of the four years as stated in the Stipulation and to align

 3              with affordability for rate payers.

 4


 5                              TREATMENT OF FEDERAL TAX CREDITS

 6                      A. Return on Deferred Tax Asset from Solar Production Tax Credits

 7   Q.         What did SPS originally request regarding the return on a DTA?

 8   A.         SPS anticipates that there will be a running balance of PTCs from SPS-owned solar

 9              generation facilities that have been passed on to customers but not yet sold to buyers in the

10              tax credit market. SPS originally requested to earn a return on this balance at its requested

11              weighted average cost of capital (“WACC”) of 8.21%. SPS also originally requested that

12              the return be collected through base rates or alternatively flowed through the FPPCAC

13              (“Fuel Clause”), calling this “an alternative cost recovery mechanism for the tax credit

14              value and costs.”1

15   Q.         What did the Final Order in case 24-00270-UT, SPS’s most recent FPPCAC case,

16              conclude regarding a return on the solar PTC DTA?

17   A.         Both the Final Order as well as the Comprehensive Nonunanimous Stipulation from the

18              24-00270-UT case state, “To the extent SPS does not transfer PTCs associated with the

19              SPS Self-Build Solar Projects, SPS may accrue a DTA and recover a return on the DTA




     1
         Direct Testimony of Zoe Lees. Page 85, lines 12-13.

                                                               3
                                       CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                           TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO STIPULATION OF
                                       PETERSON BROSSY

 1           balance associated with the SPS Self-Build Solar Projects through base rates, with a rate

 2           to be determined in SPS’s next general rate case.”2

 3   Q.      Does SPS’s request to pass a return on the DTA through the FPPCAC contradict the

 4           Commission Final Order and Stipulation from 24-00270-UT?

 5   A.      Yes, SPS’s request to recover the return through the FPPCAC is contrary to the

 6           Commission’s Final Order to recover the DTA return through base rates.

 7   Q.      What does the Stipulation agree to do concerning SPS’s original request?

 8   A.      The Stipulation contains SPS’s original alternative request to pass the return on the solar

 9           DTA through the FPPCAC. The Stipulation does lower the return from the WACC to the

10           long-term cost of debt (5.29%), which is a positive adjustment in Staff’s view. It also

11           includes language reserving the right to seek different treatment of these PTCs at a future

12           proceeding. Also, and importantly, it states that “The PTC DTA attributable to the SPS

13           Solar Projects shall be excluded from rate base in future base rate proceedings.”3

14   Q.      What was Staff’s position in Direct Testimony?

15   A.      I recommended that the return on the PTC DTA balance be SPS’s weighted cost of debt of

16           2.33%. Staff believe that a lower return reduces the incentive to let the DTA balance run

17           unnecessarily large. The cost of long-term debt is a move in the right direction but does not

18           match Staff’s Direct testimony’s recommendation.




     2
       Final Order, Case 24-00270-UT, page 34, paragraph 86; Comprehensive Nonunanimous Stipulation, page 5,
     section 1.2 (B)(2) [emphasis added].
     3
       Comprehensive Stipulation, Section 1.8 (A)

                                                           4
                                          CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                              TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO STIPULATION OF
                                          PETERSON BROSSY

 1   Q.         Does Staff support the Stipulation’s treatment of the DTA return and recovery issue?

 2   A.         No, Staff does not. Staff recommends that the return on the DTA be included in base rates

 3              as approved in the 24-00270-UT Commission Final Order. Including the DTA return in the

 4              FPPCAC eliminates the risk of recovery for the utility and shifts that risk instead onto rate

 5              payers. While it is true that the DTA balance projected into the future test year could be

 6              over-estimated, there is no guarantee of recovery through base rates unlike recovery

 7              through the fuel clause. Also, Staff would note, this is an asset, which, like other regulatory

 8              assets in base rates, is appropriately included and reviewed in a base rate proceeding like

 9              this one where all relevant issues are assessed holistically. Further, the Stipulation seems

10              to also include a provision barring the PTC DTA from being considered in future base rate

11              proceedings, which Staff views as an inappropriate attempt to prevent any future

12              Commission from conducting appropriate review and assessment of recovery of DTAs.

13

14                      B. Treatment of ITCs for the Cunningham BESS and Plant X BESS

15   Q.         What is the Stipulation’s treatment for the BESS ITCs?

16   A.         In short, the parties stipulate to amortize the value of the ITCs over a five-year period; to

17              include transfer costs over the same period; to accrue a regulatory asset for transfer costs

18              capped at 10% of the ITC nominal value; and apply a return on the unamortized ITC value

19              and transfer cost balance at the agreed upon WACC.4




     4
         Comprehensive Stipulation, Section 1.8 (B)

                                                          5
                                           CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                               TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO STIPULATION OF
                                           PETERSON BROSSY

 1   Q.         Does Staff support the Stipulation’s treatment of this issue?

 2   A.         Staff does support most of the Stipulation provisions on this issue, with the exception of

 3              the WACC return on the transfer costs. As stated in my Direct Testimony, I recommend

 4              that transfer cost balances related to ITCs do not earn any carrying charge, in other words

 5              no return on the transfer costs. Staff maintains, as stated in my Direct testimony, that it is

 6              reasonable for the Company to perform its operations relating to the sale of investment tax

 7              credits, and to recover those costs from customers without expecting additional return in

 8              the form of carrying charges.5

 9

10                                   C. PTC Transfer Costs for Hale and Sagamore

11   Q.         What is the Stipulation treatment regarding transfer costs for Hale and Sagamore?

12   A.         SPS requested to recover PTC transfer costs through the FPPCAC capped at 10% of the

13              nominal value.

14   Q.         Does the request differ from SPS’s original request?

15   A.         No, it does not.

16   Q.         What does Staff recommend at this time?




     5
         Direct Testimony of Peterson Brossy, page 25.

                                     PETERSON BROSSY

 1   A.   In case 24-00270-UT the Commission approved these costs with the same 10% cap through

 2        the FPPCAC for SPS’s solar projects. Staff does not oppose this provision of the

 3        Stipulation.

 4


 5                                  RATE CASE EXPENSES

 6   Q.   What did SPS originally request regarding Rate Case Expenses?

 7   A.   SPS requested to recover $4,614,630 in total Rate Case Expenses, amortized over a two-

 8        year period for $2,307,315 expense in the Revenue Requirement. While SPS attachment

 9        ZEL-7 showed a total expense of $4,342,330, the jurisdictional cost of service model

10        included an amount for Rate Case Expenses of $2,307,315, which indicates a $4,614,630

11        total when multiplied by two to correspond with the amortization period.

12   Q.   What does the Stipulation request for Rate Case Expenses?

13   A.   The Stipulation includes recovery for $4,342,331 in rate case expenses.

14   Q.   What does Staff recommend?

15   A.   As in Staff’s position in Direct testimony, Staff recommends a total rate case expense

16        amount of $3,346,476 amortized over three years instead of two, for an annual expense of

17        $1,115,492.

18   Q    Why does Staff believe a $3,346,476 amount is reasonable?

19   A.   Staff reduced SPS’s $4.3 million as follows: $230k in unsupported company expenses

20        labeled “Other”, unreasonable consultant travel expenses. Staff also observed that in its
                                                   7
                                   CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                       TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO STIPULATION OF
                                   PETERSON BROSSY

 1        two prior rate case filings SPS only incurred 74% of costs that they requested. Staff

 2        therefore reduced the 2025 FTY expense (the current case expense included as compared

 3        to the prior RFP, IRP and Standby case expenses included in the total rate case expense)

 4        by 26%. When taken together these adjustments reduce the total rate case expense to the

 5        above $3.346 million amount. In addition, Staff believes that a three-year amortization

 6        period instead of SPS’s proposed two-year period is more reasonable and increases

 7        affordability.

 8



 9                         REGULATORY ASSETS AND DEFERRALS

10           A. A Four-year Amortization of the Remaining Investment in Legacy Meters
11   Q.   What did SPS originally request regarding Legacy Meters?

12   A.   SPS originally requested to recover the remaining balance of its investment in legacy

13        meters over two years. The Company forecasted the balance in November 2027 as

14        $13,464,642, and dividing that amount by two equals a $6,732,321 annual amortization

15        expense included in the revenue requirement.

16   Q.   What does the Stipulation agree to do with this request?

17   A.   The Stipulation proposes a four-year amortization period for the legacy meter regulatory

18        asset amount. The Signatories also agree that if there remains an unamortized balance at

19        the time of subsequent rate case, SPS may include that balance for continued recovery.

20   Q.   What did Staff recommend in Direct testimony regarding this request?


                                                   8
                                   CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                       TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO STIPULATION OF
                                   PETERSON BROSSY

 1   A.   Staff recommended an amortization period of five years in order to allow the Company to

 2        recoup costs in a timely manner but also not burden rate payers with unnecessarily higher

 3        costs and to promote affordable rates.

 4   Q.   Does Staff support the Stipulation’s treatment of this issue?

 5   A.   Staff does not oppose but also does not fully support this term in the Stipulation. While it

 6        is a move in the right direction, the Signatories’ proposed amortization expense of

 7        $3,366,161 is still $673,232 higher than the $2,692,928 expense that Staff recommends

 8        and therefore does not promote affordable rates.

 9               B. A Four-year Amortization of the Community Solar Program Costs

10   Q.   What was SPS’ original request for Solar Program Costs?

11   A.   The Company requested that the $906,791 of IT costs be amortized over two years, and

12        $265,322 of “O&M” costs be added for a total of $718,717 of annual expense in the

13        revenue requirement.

14   Q.   What was Staff’s recommendation in Direct Testimony?

15   A.   I recommended that the $265,322 amount be disallowed because it was unsupported.

16   Q.   What does the Stipulation agree to do with this request?

17   A.   The Stipulation adopts a four-year amortization period for these costs.

18   Q.   How does Staff take the new request?

19   A.   Staff does not oppose but also does not fully support this term in the Stipulation. Staff

20        believes the Stipulation goes in the right direction. Assuming the total $906k IT cost

                                                    9
                                   CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                       TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO STIPULATION OF
                                   PETERSON BROSSY

 1        amount stays the same, amortized over four years and added to the “O&M” amount, the

 2        total will be about $492,000 of expense. However, the Stipulation does not mitigate

 3        Staff’s original concerns raised in Direct testimony regarding the lack of support for the

 4        O&M costs.

 5


 6                                         CONCLUSION

 7   Q.   Do you have any concluding remarks?

 8   A.   Yes. As discussed above, while there is movement toward Staff’s position on some issues,

 9        there are fundamental concerns based upon Staff’s public interest goal of promoting

10        affordable rates, that Staff identified in Direct testimony that are still not addressed,

11        including the proposed revenue requirement total amount. Staff stands by these positions

12        and judges them the appropriate basis for Commission decisions in this rate case.

13

14   Q.   Does this conclude your testimony?

15   A.   Yes.
